title: "Installing Git"

# Installing Git

After this page you have a current `git` on your `PATH` on Linux and can print its version.

## Check what you already have

```bash
git --version
which -a git
```

This book wants **2.45 or newer** on **Linux**. Examples were checked against **2.55**. You need `git switch`, `git restore`, and (later) SSH commit signing.

Most desktop distros already ship a new enough Git. If `which git` prints `/usr/bin/git` and the version is 2.45+, you are done.

## Install from the distro

**Arch Linux and Omarchy**

```bash
pacman -Q git
# missing or too old:
sudo pacman -S git
```

**Debian and Ubuntu**

```bash
sudo apt update
sudo apt install git
```

**Fedora**

```bash
sudo dnf install git
```

Enterprise images sometimes freeze Git at 2.25. If `git --version` is older than 2.45, use your distro’s backports or a current tarball from [git-scm.com](https://git-scm.com/downloads) so `switch` and `restore` exist.

## Line endings and the filesystem

Linux stores **LF** line endings and executable bits. Leave `core.autocrlf` unset. Leave `core.fileMode` at the default (`true`) so `chmod +x` is recorded. Those defaults are why hooks and scripts in later chapters work with `chmod +x hook.sh`.

## What else you need for Parts I–II

| Tool | Role |
|------|------|
| A Linux terminal | Where you run `git` (`bash` or another POSIX shell) |
| A text editor | `nvim` in this book’s config examples; any editor is fine |

Docker, Kubernetes, and a forge account wait until later parts.

Set `core.editor` once you know which editor you type in (next page). Until then, `git commit -m "message"` avoids opening one.

## Confirm

```bash
git --version
which git
echo "$HOME"
```

`$HOME` should be `/home/<you>`. Then set identity and the three config layers on the next page.
